title: How to Harvest Vocab Words
transcript:
0:00
How to harvest vocab, also known as where's my word list? Ellen, just give me a word list of vocab that will definitely appear on my actual LSAT.

0:12
Please be precognitive. Also, please know which words I know and don't. That word list doesn't exist, friends. I do have a lot of word lists that my students have made over the years and that sort of thing.

0:23
But here's the thing. No word list I could ever give you would ever be as good, even remotely, as the one that you make yourself.

0:32
And so that's why I want to teach you how to harvest vocab to make your own word list that's going to be perfectly customized to exactly your unique history of knowing words and not knowing words.

0:43
And so very briefly, I'll just tell you kind of how I implemented this in my own life and how I built my own vocabulary.

0:51
And so when I was young, I was briefly homeschooled for two years. And in the seventh and eighth grade, I read a lot of the Folger Shakespeare editions.

1:02
And the cool thing about the Folger Shakespeare editions was that on every page, it's like the text of Shakespeare. And then on the left side would be all these word definitions.

1:11
So it would just be a bold and then the definition, bold definition of words that appeared on the actual play on the other side of the page.

1:16
And I thought this was like the coolest thing in the world. And so I as I would go through, I would just read like the definitions page as like part of the play.

1:27
You know, I even if I thought maybe I knew what the word was or something, I was very, very curious about the words

1:33
and I like wanted to learn them the way I wanted to learn about the play. And so I gradually built my vocab knowledge in context of the words that I was seeing on those pages.

1:43
And of course, this is before, you know, I was like with a computer spreadsheet and all that kind of stuff.

1:49
And so I did not have a really like systematized way of learning, but I gathered those words as I go.

1:54
And as I saw them come back and come back and come back, I gradually incorporated them into my just verbal lexicon.

2:00
And so I want to show you how you can be harvesting words when they aren't, you know, as conveniently highlighted and defined for you like the brilliant Folger Shakespeare edition.

2:10
So as you're going through your Extracurricular Reading, your actual LSAT practice in a section, real life conversations with people and especially the guide for essential knowledge in your Extracurricular Reading is especially good for this. I really want you to just take notes or highlights of

2:29
words that you don't know. And so the reason why we want you to be the one to highlight is because we don't want to add words to the list that are superfluous, that are words that you already would have known and they're just kind of wasting your time hanging out on the list. And maybe we

2:45
wouldn't have known to add a certain word to your vocab list that you didn't know. Maybe you just never enCountered it before, but it didn't seem like, oh, this is the most common word or something.

2:56
That's how things might get left out of your understanding, which obviously no one wants. And so the way that you do this mechanically can vary.

3:03
Sure, if you're in a conversation, maybe taking a quick note in like Apple Notes or Google Notes or whatever Google Notes even exists, a notion, Google Doc, whatever

3:13
of words that you're hearing in conversation. But then if it's something like in a Kindle, for instance, you can click define and you can like send it to I think even save the words like a vocab list from Kindle, I believe.

3:25
But I want this all, no matter how you gather it casually, to centralize eventually into a spreadsheet where you just write down words that you don't know.

3:36
And so if in a conversation you're just jotting things down in random notes or saving them in Kindle or whatever, I do want you at the end of the day to just copy paste them into this spreadsheet.

3:46
It's really nice to have these words in the spreadsheet because it's just a really convenient way to organize information, to Write In definitions, Write In examples and even copy paste into an AI or upload the sheet itself into an AI.

4:00
So it's really easy and portable for us to use it. That's why we want to eventually get everything into a spreadsheet.

4:05
But as you're going throughout your practice, keep that bar to get into the spreadsheet really low. Like, for instance, if you look at a word and you're like, OK, I got 80, 90 percent knows know what that means. That's not good enough.

4:20
If I want you to put every single word that you are not absolutely 100 percent sure of into that word list, because the LSAT will often play on the ambiguity that's left over in that last 10 to 20 percent of uncertainty in a word where if you're saying a logical reasoning question, oh, well,

4:40
is that meaning really the same? Like, I'm not sure. That's the last 10 to 20 percent. If you can be absolutely sure that you know what the word means, then we're in business.

4:50
And of course, if you're 80 or 90 percent sure you throw it into your spreadsheet, you do some review later and you're like, yeah, oh, I was right. OK,

4:56
yeah, that is exactly what it is. The confidence that we gain in our lexicon from doing that is invaluable,

5:03
even if it was just confirming our previous definition, because we would have brought that uncertainty into the actual test itself had we not confirmed it.

5:11
And so that's why I want you to throw stuff in there that even if you're basically, you know, think it's probably this, it still goes in your word list.

5:21
Awesome. OK, well, I can't wait to talk about how you're going to learn these words both with and without AI.

5:26
See you in a second.
